title: What is Terraform, how does the plan/apply workflow work, and why do we use Infrastructure as Code?
shortTitle: Terraform — plan/apply workflow and why we use Infrastructure as Code

s1_definition.profdef: Terraform is an open-source Infrastructure as Code tool from HashiCorp that lets you declare your cloud infrastructure — servers, databases, networks, load balancers — in human-readable configuration files written in HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language). You describe the desired end state, and Terraform figures out the exact API calls needed to reach that state. It keeps a state file that records what it has already created, compares your desired configuration against reality, and applies only the difference.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India wants to open a new branch. The old way is like calling the carpenter, the electrician, and the painter one by one, telling each of them verbally what to do, and hoping nobody forgets anything. Infrastructure as Code is like writing one detailed blueprint that says "this branch needs two teller counters, one vault, three ATMs, and this exact network layout." Terraform reads that blueprint and builds everything exactly as written. If next month you add a line saying "one more ATM," Terraform sees that only the ATM is new and installs just that, touching nothing else. The blueprint is the source of truth, so every branch comes out identical and you never rely on someone's memory.
s1_definition.oneliner: Terraform turns infrastructure into a version-controlled blueprint, and plan shows you the diff before apply makes it real.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Terraform is an open-source Infrastructure as Code tool from HashiCorp that lets you declare your cloud infrastructure — servers, databases, networks, load balancers — in human-readable configuration files written in HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language). You describe the desired end state, and Terraform figures out the exact API calls needed to reach that state. It keeps a state file that records what it has already created, compares your desired configuration against reality, and applies only the difference.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India wants to open a new branch. The old way is like calling the carpenter, the electrician, and the painter one by one, telling each of them verbally what to do, and hoping nobody forgets anything. Infrastructure as Code is like writing one detailed blueprint that says "this branch needs two teller counters, one vault, three ATMs, and this exact network layout." Terraform reads that blueprint and builds everything exactly as written. If next month you add a line saying "one more ATM," Terraform sees that only the ATM is new and installs just that, touching nothing else. The blueprint is the source of truth, so every branch comes out identical and you never rely on someone's memory.

**One line to remember:** Terraform turns infrastructure into a version-controlled blueprint, and plan shows you the diff before apply makes it real.

sections.s2_technical:
Terraform is declarative. You do not write step-by-step instructions like "first create the VPC, then the subnet, then the server." Instead you declare what you want to exist, and Terraform builds a dependency graph and decides the correct order itself. For example, a block that declares an AWS RDS database for the bank's transaction records looks like `resource "aws_db_instance" "transactions" { engine = "postgres" instance_class = "db.r6g.large" allocated_storage = 100 }`. You never say how to create it; you only say what it should be.

The heart of Terraform is the state file, usually named `terraform.tfstate`. This file is Terraform's memory. It records every real resource Terraform has created and maps it back to your configuration. When you run Terraform again, it reads the state, calls the cloud provider to check current reality, compares both against your `.tf` files, and computes the difference. Without state, Terraform would have no way of knowing that the database it is looking at is the same one it made last week.

The `terraform plan` command is the dry run. It computes what Terraform intends to do and prints it as a diff. A plus sign means a resource will be created, a tilde means it will be modified in place, a minus sign means it will be destroyed, and a minus-slash-plus means it will be destroyed and recreated. For a bank this preview is essential — you absolutely want to see "this will DESTROY the production transactions database" before it happens. The plan changes nothing; it only reports.

The `terraform apply` command executes the plan. By default it shows the same diff again and waits for you to type `yes`. Once confirmed, it makes the real API calls, creates or changes resources, and updates the state file to match the new reality. In a pipeline you usually run `terraform plan -out=tfplan` to save the plan to a file, then `terraform apply tfplan` to apply exactly that saved plan, so nothing can drift between the preview and the execution.

Why Infrastructure as Code matters is the deeper point. Everything is version-controlled in Git, so you get the full history of who changed what and why, and you can roll back. The configuration is repeatable, so the staging environment is byte-for-byte identical to production, which eliminates the classic "it worked in staging" surprise. It is self-documenting, because the `.tf` files ARE the documentation of your infrastructure. And it supports peer review — infrastructure changes go through a pull request just like application code, so a second engineer sees "you are about to resize the production database" before it ships.

A senior-level nuance is drift. Drift happens when someone changes a resource manually in the cloud console, so reality no longer matches the state file. The next `terraform plan` detects this and shows the drift as a diff, and `terraform apply` will revert the manual change back to what the code says. This is why disciplined teams forbid manual console edits — the code must always be the single source of truth.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India is launching a new microservice called the account-ledger-service that stores every account's running balance. The platform team must provide the cloud infrastructure for it: a PostgreSQL database to hold the ledger, and a storage bucket to hold daily balance-snapshot files for audit.

Problem 1 — the bank used to create databases by hand in the AWS console. One engineer created the staging database with 20 GB of storage and another created production with 100 GB, and the versions differed. When a bug only appeared in production, nobody could reproduce it in staging because the two environments were not actually the same. This is exactly the problem Infrastructure as Code solves — when both environments come from the same code with only a size variable changed, they are guaranteed consistent.

Problem 2 — last quarter an engineer meant to delete a test database but, because he was clicking through the console tired at midnight, he nearly deleted the production ledger. There was no preview, no second pair of eyes, no undo. This is exactly what `terraform plan` prevents — it prints "this will DESTROY aws_db_instance.ledger" in red before anything happens, and the change goes through a pull request so a teammate reviews it first.

Problem 3 — when auditors asked "who changed the database backup retention from 7 days to 1 day, and when," nobody could answer because console clicks leave no readable history. With Terraform in Git, the answer is one `git blame` away.

The mini-project is a Terraform configuration that declares the ledger database and the audit bucket, uses variables so staging and production differ only by size, and demonstrates the plan-then-apply workflow. We will show the folder structure, the configuration files, the variable files per environment, and the exact commands. We will also include a small Java snippet showing how the running service reads the database endpoint that Terraform produced as an output.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
account-ledger-infra/
├── main.tf                      (resource declarations)
├── variables.tf                 (input variable definitions)
├── outputs.tf                   (values exported after apply)
├── versions.tf                  (terraform + provider version pins)
├── envs/
│   ├── staging.tfvars           (staging-specific values)
│   └── production.tfvars        (production-specific values)
└── README.md

account-ledger-service/          (the Java app that consumes the infra)
└── src/main/java/com/bank/ledger/
    └── config/DataSourceConfig.java
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Initialize: download the AWS provider plugin and set up the backend.
terraform init

# Format and validate the configuration before anything else.
terraform fmt -recursive
terraform validate

# PLAN for staging — this ONLY previews, changes nothing.
# Save the plan to a file so apply runs exactly what we reviewed.
terraform plan -var-file=envs/staging.tfvars -out=staging.tfplan

# Review the diff. '+' create, '~' modify, '-' destroy. Then APPLY.
terraform apply staging.tfplan

# Promote to production — SAME code, different variable file.
terraform plan -var-file=envs/production.tfvars -out=prod.tfplan
# A teammate reviews prod.tfplan in the pull request BEFORE this runs:
terraform apply prod.tfplan

# See the exported endpoint the Java service needs:
terraform output ledger_db_endpoint
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: an engineer adds `backup_retention_days = 30` to `envs/production.tfvars` for the ledger database, replacing the old value of 7.

Step 1: The engineer runs `terraform plan -var-file=envs/production.tfvars`. Terraform reads the `.tf` files to learn the desired state and reads `terraform.tfstate` to learn what it created last time. The desired state now says 30 days; the state file says 7 days.

Step 2: Terraform calls the AWS API to confirm the real database currently has 7 days of retention, so reality and state agree. It computes the difference between desired (30) and current (7).

Step 3: Terraform prints a diff showing `~ backup_retention_period = 7 -> 30` with a tilde, meaning this is an in-place modification, not a destroy-and-recreate. The engineer confirms this is a safe change — resizing retention does not drop the database.

Step 4: The plan is saved to `prod.tfplan` and opened as a pull request. A second engineer reviews it, sees only the retention change and nothing destructive, and approves.

Step 5: The pipeline runs `terraform apply prod.tfplan`. Terraform makes the single AWS API call to change retention to 30 days. It then updates `terraform.tfstate` so the state file now records 30 days, keeping memory and reality in sync.

Step 6: The next `terraform plan` shows "No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration," confirming the loop is closed.

```
Oct 24, 2026 11:10:02 PM INFO: terraform plan started (production)
Oct 24, 2026 11:10:05 PM INFO: aws_db_instance.ledger will be updated in-place
Oct 24, 2026 11:10:05 PM INFO:   ~ backup_retention_period: 7 -> 30
Oct 24, 2026 11:10:05 PM INFO: Plan: 0 to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy
Oct 24, 2026 11:12:40 PM INFO: aws_db_instance.ledger: Modifications complete
Oct 24, 2026 11:12:40 PM INFO: Apply complete! 0 added, 1 changed, 0 destroyed
Oct 24, 2026 11:12:41 PM INFO: state file updated: backup_retention_period=30
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Engineer edits envs/production.tfvars: backup_retention_days 7 -> 30
    │
    ▼
  terraform plan -var-file=envs/production.tfvars
    │ reads .tf files      -> desired state (30 days)
    │ reads tfstate        -> last-known state (7 days)
    │ calls AWS API        -> real state (7 days)
    │ computes diff        -> "~ 7 -> 30" (in-place modify)
    ▼
  Plan saved to prod.tfplan  ──pull request──→  Reviewer approves
    │
    ▼
  terraform apply prod.tfplan
    │ AWS ModifyDBInstance(backup_retention_period=30)
    ▼
  Real RDS updated: retention = 30 days
    │
    ▼
  terraform.tfstate updated: 7 -> 30  (memory matches reality)
    │
    ▼
  Next plan: "No changes. Infrastructure matches configuration."
```

```
  ┌─ Design Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  DRY: one main.tf, environments differ only by .tfvars        │

                                 ┌───────────────────┐

                                 │ aws_db_instance   │◆ owns config
                                 │ aws_s3_bucket     │◆ owns config
                                 │ public_access_blk │───▶ references bucket

                                           ▼
                                 ┌───────────────────┐
                                 │ outputs.tf        │
                                 │ ledger_db_endpoint│───▶ consumed by Java app
                                 │ snapshot_bucket   │
                                 └───────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: a Resource's Lifecycle ──────────────────

  [not in state] ──apply(create)──→ [tracked, matches] 
        │                                  │
        │                                  │ config changed
        │                                  ▼
        │                          [plan shows ~ diff]
        │                                  │ apply
        │                                  ▼
        │                          [tracked, matches]
        │                                  │ resource removed from .tf
        │                                  ▼
        └────────────────────────── [plan shows - destroy] ──apply──→ [not in state]

  ── Call Chain (plan/apply) ────────────────────────────────

  1. terraform init        → download aws provider, configure backend
  2. terraform plan        → load .tf + .tfvars  (desired)
  3.   → read tfstate       (last known)
  4.   → refresh via AWS API (real)
  5.   → compute diff       (desired vs real)
  6.   → write plan file    prod.tfplan
  7. terraform apply plan  → execute AWS API calls in dependency order
  8.   → update tfstate     (memory = reality)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Terraform is HashiCorp's Infrastructure as Code tool. Instead of clicking through a cloud console to create servers and databases, you declare the desired end state in configuration files, and Terraform works out the exact API calls needed to reach that state. It is declarative, so you say what you want to exist rather than the steps to build it, and it maintains a state file that is its memory of everything it has already created.

The workflow has two core steps. The plan command is a dry run — it reads your configuration, reads the state file, checks the real cloud, and prints a diff showing exactly what it will create, change, or destroy, without touching anything. The apply command then executes that plan and updates the state file to match the new reality. In practice I save the plan to a file with plan dash out and apply that exact file, so nothing can change between the review and the execution.

In my work at National Bank of India I used Terraform to manage the infrastructure for an account ledger service — a PostgreSQL database and an encrypted audit bucket. The real value showed up in three ways. First, staging and production came from the same code with only a variable file differing, so the environments were genuinely identical and bugs stopped hiding. Second, every change went through a pull request where a teammate could see a plan that said in plain text "this will destroy the production database" before anything ran — that preview has prevented real accidents. Third, because everything lived in Git, when auditors asked who changed the backup retention and when, the answer was one git blame away.

The concept I always stress is drift. If someone edits a resource by hand in the console, reality no longer matches the state file, and the next plan immediately shows that drift as a diff. That is why disciplined teams forbid manual console edits — the code must be the single source of truth. Infrastructure as Code gives you repeatability, version history, peer review, and self-documenting infrastructure, which is exactly what a bank needs where a single mistake can affect customer money.
